extracted.intended_audience: the people of the State of New York / citizens concerned with the Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative commentary on how the Constitution should allocate the power to regulate federal elections (times, places, manner), weighing risks of lodging that power in state versus national legislatures and recommending structural safeguards. Focused political-theory analysis aimed at persuading citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must contain means of its own preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: EVERY GOVERNMENT OUGHT TO CONTAIN IN ITSELF THE MEANS OF ITS OWN PRESERVATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a fundamental design principle: structures and powers should be allocated so that the government can protect and maintain its own existence; departures from this rule should only be made out of necessity to incorporate other indispensable ingredients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of election-regulating power: local first, national ultimate
rubrics_metrics.description: A discretionary power over elections ought either to be lodged wholly in the national legislature, wholly in the State legislatures, or primarily in the latter and ultimately in the former; the convention preferred the last mode — submit regulation to local administrations in the first instance, reserve national right to interpose when necessary for safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance convenience and local satisfaction with an ultimate national backstop: ordinarily let states regulate (for convenience), but reserve national authority to act under extraordinary circumstances threatening the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of exclusive state control over federal elections
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive power of regulating elections for the national government in the hands of the State legislatures would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy — they could at any moment annihilate it by neglecting to provide for choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate constitutional allocations by the conceivable worst-case consequences (even if unlikely): if state control could theoretically prevent federal elections, that risk argues against exclusive state authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule as fundamental; avoid supermajority/quorum traps
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring more than a majority for a quorum, or more than a majority of a quorum for a decision, would reverse the fundamental principle of free government — the majority would no longer rule; power would be transferred to the minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Against procedural devices that empower minorities (e.g., inflated quorum rules or supermajority requirements) because they obstruct passage of laws needed for justice or the general good and facilitate obstructionism and secessionist practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid defensive privileges limited to particular cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If defensive privileges (higher thresholds) were limited to particular cases, an interested minority might take advantage to screen themselves from equitable sacrifices to the general weal or to extort unreasonable indulgences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not carve out narrow procedural shields that specific factions can exploit; broad application or none is preferable to selective exemptions that enable minority entrenchment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent facilitation of secession through procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules that foster or facilitate the practice of secessions are baneful — such practices lead directly to public convulsions and the ruin of popular governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing election rules and procedures, avoid mechanisms that make secession or quiet disintegration of the Union practicable (e.g., repeated failures to hold elections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of congressional authority over elections (times, places, manner)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The TIMES, PLACES, and MANNER of holding elections for senators and representatives shall be prescribed in each State by the legislature thereof; but the Congress may, at any time, by law, make or alter SUCH REGULATIONS, except as to the PLACES of choosing senators."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the constitutional grant: national authority is limited to regulating times, places, and manner (with an explicit exception regarding places for choosing senators); interpret and apply that scope narrowly as a textual limit on federal intrusion into qualifications or other matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity in time of elections as a public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in the time of elections for the federal House of Representatives may be of great importance: it secures against the perpetuation of the same spirit in the body and is a cure for the diseases of faction; it enables total dissolution/renovation at once rather than gradual accretions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor uniform election timing to avoid staggered contagion of factional spirit, to enable coordinated rotation, and to facilitate regular legislative assembly; weigh convenience but prefer national uniformity for these systemic benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of selection mechanisms reduces collusion risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissimilarity in how branches are constituted (House by direct election, Senate by state legislatures, President by electors) forms a powerful obstacle to a concert of views in any partial scheme of elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design multi-modal selection processes (different electorates and methods) to prevent coordinated partiality across branches; structural variety decreases probability of a sustained common bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural safeguards (senate term length, rotation, small per-state representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate's six-year terms, rotation by thirds, no more than two senators per State, and small quorum make it unlikely that a temporary combination of a few States could annul its existence or impair its activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use term lengths, staggered rotation, and limited per-unit representation as design tools to blunt short-term conspiracies and to ensure institutional continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility of polling places affects suffrage and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Confining places of election to particular districts would make remote electors unlikely to vote; an inconvenient distance (twenty miles or twenty thousand miles) has the same discouraging effect — place restrictions can concentrate electoral power in urban locales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When regulating places of election, prioritize accessibility; rules that make voting remote will effectively disenfranchise outlying voters and can shift influence to inhabitants near the designated places.

rubrics_metrics.name: To privilege a class (wealthy) requires voter/office-holder qualifications, not place rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of securing to the rich the preference apprehended, but by prescribing qualifications of property either for those who may elect or be elected; confining places of election alone will not reliably secure such a preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques that fear place-of-election manipulation to favor a class misunderstand mechanisms of political exclusion: explicit qualifications (property or franchise limits) are the real instruments of class preference, and the constitutional power at issue does not include altering qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare federal proposals to state practices for consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: If State constitutions allow wide latitude in elections, objections to similar latitude in the federal plan are suspect; one must show why representatives of a single State are inherently more impregnable to lust of power than representatives of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposed federal rules in the context of existing state practices: inconsistent condemnation is weak unless a convincing distinction is shown; use comparative evidence from state constitutions to gauge real risks.
